summary:
Sections 430 and 431 of the Criminal Code criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Section 431, covering "unnatural crime," carries a maximum penalty of ten years' imprisonment for male same-sex acts. Section 430 addresses "grossly indecent acts" between men. A gender-neutral grossly indecent act provision reaches same-sex conduct committed willfully in public. These provisions remain in force.

United States Department of State reporting for 2023 records that the criminalising provisions are not enforced in practice, and reports no arbitrary killings, torture or enforced disappearances in Grenada that year. The absence of enforcement does not remove the exposure: the statutes remain in force with custodial penalties attached.

No legal gender recognition is available. A trans visitor's passport or other identity documents will carry the sex marker assigned at birth or issued by another jurisdiction, and there is no domestic procedure to amend it.

National law provides no protection against discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. The 1973 Constitution contains no equality clause and no protection of privacy.

LGBTIQ people face discrimination in housing, education, employment and public services, and fear of prosecution inhibits reporting to police, which affects residents and visitors alike.

Grenada does not recognise same-sex unions in any form, whether marriage or partnership. A trans visitor whose relationship would be read as same-sex under local birth-sex classification has no route to spousal recognition, and no spousal protections follow from it.
tangentialFactors:
The 1973 Constitution contains no equality or privacy clause, and the sources identify no constitutional challenge to Sections 430 and 431.

Sections 431 and 430 are framed around male same-sex acts, while the public indecency provision is gender-neutral in its wording, so the provision a trans visitor could face depends on how local law reads their sex.

Reform advocacy has been public but has not produced legislation. In May 2013 the President of the Senate publicly called for reconsideration of the ban, saying "the day is fast approaching" for repeal; the sources record no repeal or amendment since.
localsOnly:
GrenCHAP has provided services for more than 15 years to LGBTIQ+ people, people living with HIV, sex workers and vulnerable young people, and is the only local service provider named in the sources.

Discrimination in housing, education, employment and public services is documented, with no anti-discrimination or harassment law under which to complain.

Fear of prosecution inhibits reporting to police.

Households headed by same-sex couples are not eligible for any of the rights granted to opposite-sex married couples.
outOfScopeNotes:
The gender-neutral grossly indecent act provision is cited as Section 430 in some sources and as Section 7 in others; the numbering is unresolved here.

No prosecution, conviction or sentencing data for Sections 430 and 431 appears in the sources. The finding that the provisions are not enforced rests on a single government human-rights report covering 2023.

No information is available on how police, immigration or border officers treat trans travellers, and no account of document or screening practice at ports of entry is present in the sources.

No trans-specific violence data for Grenada appears in the sources; the 2023 report records no arbitrary killings, torture or enforced disappearances.

No information is available on access to hormone therapy, surgery or other trans-specific healthcare.
